summary: Notes from an ISI meeting in January 1982 about addressing in computer mail. The main conclusion was to extend username@hostname to username@host.domain, where the domain can have further structure.

eli5.summary: People met to decide how email addresses should look. They agreed to add a place-name after the computer name, so addresses can have layers.

subtitle: How the Internet settled on hierarchical domain-based email addresses

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew and mail relaying became common, the simple "user@hostname" addressing scheme became inadequate. Different systems needed ways to organize hosts into domains and find mail destinations through a hierarchy.
tldr.mechanism: A meeting of Internet pioneers decided to extend addresses to "user@host.domain" with hierarchical domain structure, and to establish name servers that translate locations to addresses and publish service information.
tldr.outcome: This decision became the foundation of the modern DNS-based email addressing system. Domain names grew hierarchical, and the infrastructure evolved to support routing mail across organizational boundaries.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: USC Information Sciences Institute, Los Angeles

facts.label: Key participants
facts.value: 20 attendees from DARPA, BBN, Berkeley, CMU, MIT, ISI, and others

today: RFC 805 documents a pivotal meeting in Internet history. The hierarchical domain-based email addressing scheme adopted here became the foundation for the Domain Name System (DNS) and remains the basis for modern email addressing. Though RFC 805 itself is now historical, its decisions shaped decades of Internet infrastructure.

sections.title: The Meeting and Its Goals
sections.content:
On January 11, 1982, leaders from DARPA, BBN, UC Berkeley, CMU, COMSAT, MIT, and other research institutions met at USC Information Sciences Institute in Los Angeles to discuss addressing issues in computer mail. The meeting was called because the ARPA Internet was growing, mail relaying (forwarding mail through intermediate hosts) was becoming common, and the simple "user@hostname" format could not support the emerging structure.

The participants, including Jon Postel, Vint Cerf, and Paul Mockapetris (who would later design the Domain Name System), focused on several problems: how to organize addresses when messages must route through multiple mail servers, how to avoid the pitfalls of source routing (where the sender specifies the path), and how to ensure that reply messages reach the correct recipients.
sections.eli5: Internet experts gathered to solve a problem: the old way of addressing email was running out of room as the network grew and mail had to pass through more computers.

sections.title: The New Hierarchical Domain Structure
sections.content:
The meeting's major conclusion was to replace the simple "user@host" format with "user@host.domain", where the domain itself can be further structured hierarchically. This creates a location identifier that reads from left to right, most specific to most general.

For example, instead of just "Postel@hostname", the address might be "Postel@F.ISI.IN"—Jon Postel on host F in the ISI complex of the Internet domain. The dots in the hostname allow unlimited hierarchical nesting without changing mail software except to recognize the new syntax.

One alternative discussed was replacing "user@host" with a "unique-id@location-id" model, where each mailbox had a globally unique identifier independent of its location, and the location could change. However, the meeting recognized that the "user@host" model was too well established to change, and many systems already used dots in usernames in incompatible ways, so this idea was set aside.

The key decision was to extend only the right side of the @ symbol (the hostname part) to avoid breaking existing user naming conventions. The highest-level domain names would need to be globally unique and administratively controlled.
sections.eli5: Instead of "user@computer", addresses would become "user@computer.organization.domain". This lets each organization have its own subdomains without needing one central master list.

sections.title: Name Servers and Service Discovery
sections.content:
The meeting identified three separate functions a name server should provide. The "white pages" service allows users to look up a person by name and other properties, returning one or more matches, each with an associated unique user ID. The "unique-id to location-id" service translates a user ID to a current location (like a forward address). The "location-id to address" service converts a domain or host name into a numeric network address.

The group decided that the location-id to address service was the most urgent to define. They also discussed whether name servers should return information about which mail services a destination supports (for example, whether it accepts NCP/FTP mail, TCP/SMTP mail, or both). This information could be coded as service names or by protocol and port numbers, or it could be queried from the host itself.

For initial implementation, the meeting proposed starting with a simple text file accessible via FTP, with both connection-oriented (TCP-based) and connectionless (UDP-based) query access to a name server. This might extend the IEN-116 name server design. The group also recognized that while a central name server might be useful to start, a distributed system with servers per domain would offer better maintenance and reliability if the databases were replicated.
sections.eli5: Computers would ask a name server where to find an address, what services it offers, and how to reach it. These servers could be centralized at first, then distributed across organizations later.

sections.title: Action Items and Implementation Timeline
sections.content:
The meeting assigned specific follow-up tasks with deadlines. Dave Crocker was tasked with revising RFC 733 to include the hierarchical naming procedure by February 15, 1982. Jon Postel was assigned to specify the Host Name Server and update the NCP/TCP transition plan and SMTP specification to use the new naming convention, also by February 15. A Mail System Description was planned (deadline unspecified) to document how to use SMTP and name servers together.

The group recognized that many programs on many hosts would need modification to handle dots in the hostname field, a task assigned to "A Cast of Thousands." DARPA (Duane Adams) was given the responsibility to set a date—by March 1, 1982—after which it would be acceptable to send mail with dots in the host field across the ARPANET and Internet without complaint.
sections.eli5: Different people were assigned to update the standards, programs had to be fixed, and a date was set for when everyone could start using the new format.
